name: Portland International Airport
before:
Oregon's main airport, inside Portland's city limits just south of the Columbia River, and 12 miles by road north east of downtown. It carries 90 per cent of the state's air passengers and more than 95 per cent of its air cargo, and is a hub for Alaska Airlines.

The one fact every client appreciates: the Port of Portland requires every shop and restaurant in the airport to charge the same as it would off airport. No terminal mark-up.

That policy sits alongside some genuinely unusual amenities. There is a microcinema run by the Hollywood Theatre showing free short films by Portland filmmakers, a distillery in the terminal and local food carts before security.

There is one terminal with four concourses, B to E, and 60 gates. International flights use the Governor Victor G. Atiyeh International Concourse, part of Concourse D.

Getting into the city is simple. The MAX Red Line light rail runs from the terminal to downtown Portland and west to Beaverton.

The Oregon Air National Guard's 142nd Wing flies F-15EX Eagle IIs from the south west of the site.
after:
Oregon's main airport, about 6 miles north east of downtown Portland as the crow flies. It is a hub for Alaska Airlines.

Under a Port of Portland street pricing policy, shops and restaurants in the airport charge the same as they would outside it.

Among the amenities is a microcinema run by the Hollywood Theatre, showing free short films about the Pacific Northwest.

There is one terminal with four concourses, B to E. International flights use a section of Concourse D.

Getting into the city is simple: the MAX Red Line light rail runs from the terminal to downtown Portland.

F-15EX Eagle IIs of the Oregon Air National Guard's 142nd Wing fly from a base at the airport.

claims.claim: inside Portland's city limits just south of the Columbia River
claims.wasBefore: inside Portland's city limits just south of the Columbia River
claims.why: Only Wikipedia says so in words. The FAA record gives Portland as the associated city and Multnomah County, which is not the same as the city limits, and the operator's noise page says only that jet flight paths keep aircraft over the Columbia River.

claims.claim: 12 miles by road north east of downtown
claims.wasBefore: and 12 miles by road north east of downtown
claims.why: Fails the coordinates check (12 miles against 5.9 miles in a straight line, ratio 2.04). Corrected to about 6 miles as the crow flies (Wikipedia and the coordinates). The operator also gives 12 miles, the road distance: noted for Andy in the kept claim.

claims.claim: 90 per cent of the state's air passengers and more than 95 per cent of its air cargo
claims.wasBefore: It carries 90 per cent of the state's air passengers and more than 95 per cent of its air cargo
claims.why: No second source: the operator's pages, its 2025 audit report and the FAA record give no share. The FAA's preliminary 2025 boardings suggest the passenger share is out of date: Portland's 9,054,394 is about 81 per cent of the roughly 11.1 million boardings at Oregon's seven listed commercial airports (our sum of the FAA rows, not a published figure).

claims.wasBefore: The one fact every client appreciates
claims.why: A judgement with no source; the policy itself is kept.

claims.claim: a distillery in the terminal
claims.why: Not confirmed as current. The operator's live list of all 70 shops and restaurants (read 23 Sep 2026) has no distillery, only a Freeland Spirits shop after security, and the main terminal was rebuilt in a project finished on 30 June 2026.

claims.claim: local food carts before security
claims.why: Not confirmed as current. None of the 70 places on the operator's live list (23 Sep 2026) is a food cart; the pre-security places are in the ticket hall, the mezzanine and baggage claim.

claims.claim: 60 gates
claims.why: Only Wikipedia gives a gate count; the operator's fast facts give terminals, concourses and runways but not gates.

opinion.text: Getting into the city is simple
